info.text: Unit 25 — Reporting a near-miss or hangar incident (CEFR B2). Listening, Reading, Use of English and Vocabulary.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. Right after the torque wrench fell, what did the mechanic do first?

generalfeedback.text: The mechanic says, "so I stopped the whole task at once." Stopping the task is the correct first action, because it makes the area safe before anything else.

answer.text: Stopped the whole task at once

feedback.text: Correct — stopping the task made the area safe first.

answer.text: Carried on torquing the last few flap bolts

feedback.text: No — the mechanic stopped work; carrying on would keep the hazard live.

answer.text: Picked up the wrench and kept working nearby

feedback.text: No — the tool was quarantined and the task was stopped.

answer.text: Waited for the safety officer before doing anything

feedback.text: No — the mechanic stopped the task and barriered the area first, then reported.

name.text: L2 · Dialogue 1 · did it hit the aircraft

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. The wrench struck the aircraft structure as it fell.

generalfeedback.text: False. The mechanic says, "It landed clear of the aircraft, and fortunately nobody was walking underneath." It is still a reportable near-miss even without damage.

feedback.text: No — it landed clear of the aircraft.
Correct — the tool landed clear of the aircraft.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. Roughly how many metres did the wrench drop to the floor? (Write the number only.)

generalfeedback.text: The mechanic says the wrench "dropped roughly two metres onto the concrete hangar floor." The answer is 2.

feedback.text: Correct — about two metres.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. In how many minutes did the safety officer say the debrief would be held? (Write the number only.)

generalfeedback.text: Rita says, "we will hold a proper debrief in ten minutes." The answer is 10.

feedback.text: Correct — in ten minutes.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 2 again. What did the team finally agree was the root cause?

generalfeedback.text: They agree it "really looks like weak tool control, rather than just my tired grip" — no lanyard, poor light and a shaky stand together. The root cause is the weak system, not one person.

feedback.text: Correct — the system of tool control was weak.

answer.text: The mechanic's tired hand and nothing else

feedback.text: No — the team looked past the tired grip to the wider system.

answer.text: A faulty torque wrench from the tool store

feedback.text: No — the wrench was not blamed; tool control was.

answer.text: Bad weather outside the hangar that evening

feedback.text: No — weather is not mentioned as a cause.

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 3 again. Nobody was injured in the near-miss.

generalfeedback.text: True. Marek says, "Nobody was injured, although honestly it could have been very bad." No injury, but still a serious near-miss.

feedback.text: Correct — no one was hurt.
No — the dialogue says nobody was injured.

questiontext.text: Listen to the hangar announcement again. At what time (o'clock) will the toolbox talk be held? (Write the hour as a number.)

generalfeedback.text: The safety officer says, "We will hold a short toolbox talk at three o'clock." The answer is 3.

feedback.text: Correct — at three o'clock.

questiontext.text:
Read this tech log entry, then answer.

TECH LOG — A/C REG YL-BAK · Access stand S-14 rail found loose during panel work. Stand withdrawn from service and tagged. Raise work order for rail repair before re-use.

According to the entry, what must happen before stand S-14 is used again?

generalfeedback.text: The entry says the stand is "withdrawn from service and tagged" and a work order must be raised for the rail repair before re-use. So it must be repaired first.

answer.text: The loose rail must be repaired

feedback.text: Correct — a work order for the rail repair is required first.

answer.text: The stand may be used if a mechanic is careful

feedback.text: No — it is withdrawn from service, not "use with care".

answer.text: The whole aircraft must be moved to another bay

feedback.text: No — the entry is about the stand, not the aircraft.

answer.text: The safety officer must sign the tech log twice

feedback.text: No — no such step is mentioned.

questiontext.text: Read the tech log entry in R1 again. Stand S-14 was left in service for other mechanics to use.

generalfeedback.text: False. The stand was "withdrawn from service and tagged", so it must not be used until the rail is repaired.

feedback.text: No — it was withdrawn from service.
Correct — the stand was withdrawn and tagged.

questiontext.text:
Read this Service Bulletin extract, then answer.

SB 27-118 · REASON: Several operators reported dropped tools during flap work. RECOMMENDATION: Fit a lanyard to every hand tool used above floor level. Update the task card to add a lanyard check as Step 1.

Why was this Service Bulletin issued?

generalfeedback.text: The "REASON" line states that operators reported dropped tools during flap work. The bulletin then recommends tool lanyards to prevent it.

feedback.text: Correct — that is the stated reason.

answer.text: Operators asked for a lighter type of torque wrench

feedback.text: No — the bulletin is about lanyards, not wrench weight.

answer.text: The flap panel bolts were found to be over-torqued

feedback.text: No — torque values are not the reason given.

answer.text: Inspectors found corrosion on several access stands

feedback.text: No — corrosion is not mentioned in the bulletin.

name.text: R4 · Service Bulletin · task card change

questiontext.text: Read the Service Bulletin in R3 again. The bulletin tells operators to add a lanyard check to the task card.

generalfeedback.text: True. The recommendation is to "Update the task card to add a lanyard check as Step 1." This makes tool control begin before the task.

feedback.text: Correct — a lanyard check is added as Step 1.
No — the bulletin does ask for a task-card change.

questiontext.text:
Read this note from the safety board, then answer.

REMINDER: A dropped tool is a reportable occurrence even when there is no injury and no damage. Report it to the safety officer as soon as the area is safe. Do not wait until the end of the shift.

What does the note say a mechanic must do after a dropped tool?

generalfeedback.text: The note says to "Report it to the safety officer as soon as the area is safe" and not to wait until the end of the shift. A near-miss is reportable even with no harm.

answer.text: Report it once the area is safe

feedback.text: Correct — report promptly, after making the area safe.

answer.text: Report it only if the tool caused visible damage

feedback.text: No — it is reportable even with no damage.

answer.text: Wait until the end of the shift and then report

feedback.text: No — the note says clearly not to wait.

answer.text: Ask a colleague to report it on their behalf

feedback.text: No — the reporter should report it themselves.

questiontext.text:
Write the verb in the past continuous (was / were + -ing).

I ______ (torque) the flap bolt when the wrench slipped.

generalfeedback.text: The long background action takes the past continuous: was torquing. The short interrupting event ("slipped") stays in the past simple.

feedback.text: Correct — "was" + "torquing".
Use "was torquing": was + the -ing form for the background action.

questiontext.text:
Write the verb in the past continuous.

We ______ (work) under the flap when the light failed.

generalfeedback.text: Use were working. With "we", "you" and "they" the correct form of be is "were", not "was".

feedback.text: Correct — "were" with "we".
Almost — but "we" takes "were", so "were working".
Use "were working": were + the -ing form.

questiontext.text:
Write the verb in the past continuous negative.

He ______ (not use) a lanyard at the time.

generalfeedback.text: Use was not using (or "wasn't using"). The negative goes after "was": was + not + using.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct — the short form is fine.
Use "was not using": was + not + the -ing form.

questiontext.text:
Write the missing word to make a past continuous question.

______ you checking the tech log when it happened?

generalfeedback.text: Use Were. In questions the form of be comes first: "Were you checking...?"

feedback.text: Correct — "Were you checking...?"
Almost — but "you" takes "were", so "Were you checking...?"
Use "Were" — the question begins with the form of "be".

questiontext.text:
Complete the sentence so it means the same. Use the past continuous.

The wrench slipped during my work on the bolt.
→ The wrench slipped while I ______ on the bolt.

generalfeedback.text: Use was working. "While" introduces the long background action, which takes the past continuous.

feedback.text: Correct — "while I was working".
Use "was working": while + past continuous for the background.

questiontext.text:
Complete the term from the vocabulary bank.

The first, real reason a problem happened is the root ______.

generalfeedback.text: The term is root cause — the first, real reason, not just a surface symptom.

feedback.text: Correct — "root cause".
The word is "cause": the root cause is the first, real reason.

questiontext.text:
Complete the term from the vocabulary bank.

A step taken before a problem, to stop it starting, is a ______ action.

generalfeedback.text: The term is preventive action. Compare it with a corrective action, which is taken after a problem to stop it happening again.

feedback.text: Correct — "preventive action".
The word is "preventive": it acts before the problem starts.

questiontext.text: Match each safety-reporting term to its plain meaning.

generalfeedback.text: near-miss = almost caused harm; hazard = something that could cause harm; contributing factor = helped cause it, not the main reason; observation = a fact you saw; mitigation = an action that lowers a risk.

answer.text: an event that almost caused harm, but did not
something that helped cause the event, not the main reason
a fact you saw or heard, not an opinion
an action that lowers a risk

questiontext.text: Match each term to the phrase it belongs in.

generalfeedback.text: These are the natural collocations from the unit: report a near-miss, find the root cause, agree a corrective action, clip a lanyard, hold a debrief.

questiontext.text: Which word means "an event that almost caused harm, but did not"?

generalfeedback.text: A near-miss is an event that almost caused harm but did not. A dropped tool that hits no one is a classic near-miss.

feedback.text: Correct.
No — that is a step taken to stop a problem happening again.
No — that is the order in which things happened.
No — that is something that helped cause the event.

questiontext.text: FOD means "foreign object debris" — loose items that can damage an aircraft.

generalfeedback.text: True. FOD is foreign object debris. A dropped tool that is left loose becomes FOD and can damage the aircraft.

feedback.text: Correct — foreign object debris.
No — FOD does stand for foreign object debris.

questiontext.text: Fitting a lanyard so a tool cannot fall again, after a dropped-tool event, is best called a...

generalfeedback.text: A step taken to stop a problem happening again is a corrective action. A preventive action is taken before any problem, to stop it starting.

feedback.text: Correct — it stops the problem happening again.
No — an observation is a fact you saw, not an action.
No — that is the order in which things happened.
No — a contributing factor is a cause, not a fix.
